sections.heading: ## Introduction
sections.replacement:
Depression is among the leading causes of years lived with disability worldwide [1], and its detection at the community and primary-care level remains incomplete. Brief self-report instruments such as the PHQ-9 enable population-scale screening [2,3], yet a fixed cut-off applied uniformly across heterogeneous populations does not prioritize those at highest risk, even where universal screening of adults is recommended [4]. Risk stratification from routinely available sociodemographic and behavioral information could support more efficient triage, and a tool restricted to self-reportable items can be delivered as a web or mobile form at low marginal cost. National health-examination and community-health surveys already collect these items and the relevant clinical ones, and community-health surveillance in particular reaches hundreds of thousands of respondents a year, an attractive development base.

ML models for depression have been developed repeatedly from large national surveys, including the KCHS and the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KNHANES) [5,6], typically reporting strong internal discrimination. Most published prediction models are assessed through internal validation alone, in depression modeling and in other clinical domains alike [7,8]. Internal performance is an optimistic indicator of real-world behavior: it does not establish that a model transports to a different sampling frame, health system, or population [9], and it does not test stability under temporal distribution shift.

The COVID-19 pandemic constitutes a natural distribution shift for mental-health prediction [10,11]: the distributions of depressive symptoms and of the associated behavioral characteristics changed, and Korean national surveillance recorded a rise in depressive symptoms and suicide attempts over the pandemic years [12]. A screening model carried into a shifted target population may show degraded calibration even where discrimination is preserved. Whether recalibration, ie, updating the intercept and slope alone [13,14], restores clinical usefulness is a practically important, under-studied question for deployed screening tools.

This study addresses these gaps by validating a KCHS-developed model in the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). Depression is operationalized identically in both surveys, minimizing outcome-harmonization error, while country, health system, racial/ethnic composition, and survey mode differ, which makes NHANES a substantively external validation set. NHANES additionally provides NCHS-defined pre- and post-pandemic data, allowing the transported model to be evaluated in two periods of the same external population; since KCHS development pools 2017-2025 and spans both, this contrasts target periods rather than validating a model frozen before the later cycle.

Two questions follow, neither settled by the models and reviews cited above [5-8]. The first is empirical: how much discrimination is lost when a model developed in one national survey is applied without refitting to another country's survey, and does that loss change across a population-wide shock such as the pandemic? The second is interpretive: when external performance falls, is the shortfall a modeling failure that better algorithms or larger training sets could recover, or a property of the transportable predictor set that no modeling effort can close? Separating the two requires more than a single external estimate. It requires an estimate of what the same predictors can achieve when a model is fitted directly inside the external population, together with a modeling search in which no external label is used for selection.

This study pursued five aims: (1) develop an ML depression-screening model in KCHS; (2) externally validate it in US NHANES (geographic transportability); (3) evaluate it separately in the pre- and post-COVID-19 cycles and quantify recalibration (transportability across target periods); (4) derive a parsimonious model for a low-burden digital tool; and (5) determine whether any residual external shortfall is closable by modeling, using a catalogued leakage-controlled optimization registry and an in-domain oracle fitted inside the external population. The pre-specified hypotheses attach to aims 1 to 4: H1 the full model achieves internal AUROC ≥0.80; H2 external discrimination remains clinically useful while calibration may deteriorate; H3 recalibration substantially improves calibration; H4 the parsimonious model incurs only a small performance loss. Aim 5 carried no numeric hypothesis and is reported as a diagnostic analysis.

## Prior-model reviews cited in the Introduction

Supports the Introduction. The Introduction states that most published prediction models are assessed through internal validation alone, in depression modeling and in other clinical domains alike, and cites two reviews for that claim [7,8]; the detailed findings of both are recorded here. A systematic review of machine-learning depression models built on electronic health records [7] found reported discrimination clustered near 0.80, with generalizability and interpretability repeatedly identified as unresolved concerns. A review of hundreds of prediction models published during the COVID-19 pandemic [8] reached the same conclusion in a different clinical domain: almost none of those models were validated in data independent of the development source, and most carried a high risk of bias. Convergence of the two reviews indicates that internal-validation-only reporting is not confined to depression modeling. The near-0.80 clustering is the benchmark against which the internal estimate of 0.836 obtained here is read under Comparison With Prior Work in the Discussion.

sections.heading: ### Study Design and Data Sources
sections.replacement:
This retrospective secondary-data study developed a clinical prediction model in one national survey and validated it, without refitting, in another. Reporting follows Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis extended to artificial intelligence (TRIPOD+AI, 2024) [15], and risk of bias was self-assessed with the Prediction model Risk Of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST) [16] as overall low-to-unclear, driven by complete-case handling of substantial and differential depression-module non-response in the external cohorts (Multimedia Appendix 1, Part B). The protocol and statistical analysis plan, including the four hypotheses, were written and dated before any analysis; the study was not registered in a public registry. A dated protocol amendment covering three of the seventeen predictors is documented under Predictors and Harmonization; the protocol, analysis plan and amendment are released unmodified with the analysis code (see Data Availability).

Development used the Korea Community Health Survey, a nationwide Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency (KDCA) survey [17] of community-dwelling adults, with annual in-person household interviews (~230,000/year) under a stratified, clustered, weighted complex-sample design; the pooled development sample was KCHS 2017-2025 records with the PHQ-9 administered (n=2,048,510). The internal split was made at cluster level (survey year crossed with design stratum crossed with primary sampling unit): the 100,001-record hold-out and the 500,000-record training set share 0 clusters. The internal estimate therefore refers to clusters the model never saw. The training-set size was fixed for computational tractability before any external evaluation (split procedure and size experiment in Multimedia Appendix 1, Part B).

External validation used NHANES, an NCHS survey combining household interview and mobile examination center assessment; depression was measured with the Depression Screener (DPQ; PHQ-9) module. NCHS documents the 2015-2018 sample design and estimation procedures [18]; the cycle-specific documentation and weight variables are named in Multimedia Appendix 1. Two periods were used as separate validation sets: pre-pandemic (2017-March 2020, "P_" files; n=7,888) and post-pandemic (August 2021-August 2023, "_L" files; n=5,210).

## Study design details: risk-of-bias domains, the internal cluster split, and released documents

Supports the Methods section Study Design and Data Sources.

The PROBAST self-assessment rated the participants, predictors and outcome domains at low risk of bias in both the development and the validation data, and the analysis domain at low risk for the development data. The analysis domain was rated unclear for the external cohorts, given that depression-module non-response was substantial and differential and was handled as complete-case (Table S8), which gives an overall low-to-unclear rating driven by that non-response.

The internal split was constructed as follows. From the pooled KCHS 2017-2025 sample of 2,048,510 records, clusters defined as survey year crossed with design stratum crossed with primary sampling unit were randomly permuted and assigned whole to the hold-out until 100,001 records had accumulated; the training set is a random 500,000-record draw from the records remaining in the clusters not assigned to the hold-out. The two sides share 0 clusters, and the hold-out spans 9,636 clusters. The internal estimate therefore refers to clusters the model never saw and not merely to new individuals within sampled clusters. The training-set size was fixed for computational tractability before any external evaluation, and a subsequent check confirmed that expanding it toward the full pooled sample did not improve, and slightly reduced, external discrimination (Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S11).

On the NHANES side, the pre-pandemic combined file and the 2021-2023 cycle carry separate NCHS documentation and weight variables, which are named in Part A.

The unmodified original protocol, statistical analysis plan, and amendment document are available with the analysis code, hyperparameter grids, and model card (see Data Availability). Part A additionally provides the year-specific harmonization crosswalk together with an English rendition of the locked amendment.

sections.heading: ### Participants and Outcome
sections.replacement:
Eligible respondents in both surveys were adults aged 20 years or older with all nine PHQ-9 items answered; pregnant respondents were retained in the main analysis. Pooling KCHS 2017-2025 gave 2,048,510 eligible records. The NHANES depression module is administered in the mobile examination center; the estimation frame is therefore the examined sample rather than the interviewed sample. Of examined adults aged 20 years or older, 7,888 pre-pandemic and 5,210 post-pandemic answered all nine items. Counts at each stage of the NHANES frame and item-level non-response are tabulated in Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S8. Predictors and outcome were recorded in the same survey contact, hence measured contemporaneously; blinding of outcome or predictor assessment does not apply to secondary analysis of already-collected survey responses.

The outcome is current depression, defined as a PHQ-9 total of at least 10 and computed identically in both surveys (nine items, scored 0 to 3, KCHS items recoded 1-4→0-3 to match NHANES). The ≥10 cut-off is the conventional screening threshold, evaluated against semi-structured diagnostic interviews in individual-participant-data meta-analyses [3,19] and validated in a Korean population [20].

sections.heading: ### Predictors and Harmonization
sections.replacement:
Only variables reducible to a common definition in both surveys entered the harmonized model, which comprised 17 predictors (Table 1). All 616 KCHS concepts were crosswalked against the NHANES codebook for both cycles; concepts were retained that are (i) available in NHANES, (ii) collected in more than one KCHS survey year, and (iii) not circular with the PHQ-9 outcome. Circular or outcome-contaminated variables were excluded a priori. Those criteria use survey documentation and variable availability only, and no NHANES outcome association was estimated for any candidate before the amendment described below was locked. The retained domains have established associations with depression in the epidemiological literature: socioeconomic position [21], sleep duration [22], physical activity [23], body mass index (BMI) [24], smoking [25], living alone [26] and partnership status [27].

BMI: body mass index.
PHQ-9: 9-item Patient Health Questionnaire.

Employment, self-rated oral health and household food insecurity entered the set through a protocol amendment written and dated before any model using those items was fitted; the study protocol had specified the other fourteen. Each addition has an established association with depression: food insecurity (pooled odds ratio ≈1.4) [28], unemployment (≈1.9-2.1) [29] and poor oral health (a bidirectional relationship) [30]. The crosswalk available when the amendment was written held a 175-variable extract, of which the seventeen predictors are every eligible concept; a later exhaustive extraction identified 265 variables common to both cycles. The deployed set is therefore exhaustive with respect to the extract available at the time of the amendment rather than with respect to the full crosswalk. Five further harmonizable items from that extraction were screened post hoc against NHANES outcome associations; none was added (Multimedia Appendix 1, Part A).

Living alone is the single retained item not present in both cycles and has no missing values anywhere in the KCHS training data; the tree learner therefore never learns a missing direction for it, and the pre-pandemic cohort is scored as if no respondent lived alone. Since availability differs between the cycles, the pandemic-period contrast is repeated with living alone removed, under Sensitivity Analyses.

Three harmonization cautions attach to the set. BMI is self-reported in KCHS, measured in NHANES. Alcohol, physical activity, and income use different instruments and were reduced to conservatively comparable definitions, only the alcohol definition being variable in sensitivity analysis. A direct Korea-US comparison using the same 18-item household module found food insecurity associated with higher odds of PHQ-9 depression in both countries, with a larger association in Korea [31]; the single-item KCHS measure used here is therefore the weakest link in the harmonized set rather than a difference in the underlying construct. Scale differences between the surveys and questionnaire discontinuities within KCHS were corrected in the analytic data before the primary analysis rather than carried as limitations; the corrections are itemized in the data-integrity audit reported below, described in Multimedia Appendix 1 and quantified singly in Table S10.

All missing-data handling was performed by a preprocessing pipeline fitted in the development training set and applied unchanged to the internal hold-out and to each external set (no leakage): Household income (within-survey quintile), self-rated health and self-rated oral health are ordinal scores and were modeled as numeric variables rather than as unordered categories, and were median-imputed and standardized. The income quintile is the one transformation not carried over unchanged, being a rank-based score recomputed within each dataset and, inside KCHS, within each survey year, since the underlying income instruments are not on a common scale. Remaining preprocessing detail, including two alternative imputation strategies examined in sensitivity analysis, is in Multimedia Appendix 1.

## Harmonization resolution, scale differences, and preprocessing detail

Supports the Methods section Predictors and Harmonization and complements the year-by-year crosswalk in Part A. 
Concept-level harmonization used a label-based per-year crosswalk on the KCHS side and cycle-specific code branching on the NHANES side. Self-rated health was harmonized to NHANES HUQ010, which corrects a file-code error in the pre-specification document, where the variable had been named HSD010/HSQ. The variables excluded a priori as circular with or contaminated by the outcome are the PHQ-9 items, suicidal ideation, the EQ-5D anxiety/depression item, the happiness index, perceived stress, and mental-health service use, the last including NHANES HUQ090 on the external side; Part A lists each exclusion with its reason.

Five further harmonizable items surfaced by the exhaustive extraction were screened after the primary analysis by comparing the direction of the adjusted association with depression across the three cohorts and then testing each item in the model. Three reversed direction between countries and the remainder added no external discrimination. That screening inspected NHANES outcome associations and is therefore a post-hoc diagnostic; no item was added, and the predictor set is unchanged.

Living alone requires a caveat that the tree learner's native missing support does not remove. Living alone has no missing values anywhere in the KCHS training data, hence the learner never observes a missing value for the item and never learns a missing direction for it. At prediction time the missing values are treated as zero and follow the same branch as "not living alone", and the pre-pandemic cohort is thus scored as if no respondent lived alone.

Of the three predictors reduced to conservatively comparable definitions, only alcohol could be varied in sensitivity analysis: the harmonized data carry a single binary physical-activity indicator and a within-survey income quintile, hence no alternative definition of those two was available. The protocol specified alcohol as current drinking plus at-risk drinking, whereas the harmonized variable uses current drinking alone, given that the NHANES quantity item was not carried through harmonization; this is recorded as a definition-level deviation in Table S9. Body mass index is self-reported in KCHS and measured in NHANES.

Two scale differences arise from NHANES top-coding. Age is capped at 80 years in NHANES, whereas 3.8% of the weighted KCHS sample is older (up to 110); the same cap was applied to KCHS before fitting, so that the model cannot separate respondents above 80 years in either survey and that part of the Korean age range is compressed. NHANES sleep duration is bounded at 2-14 hours while KCHS admits 0-23 hours, though implausible KCHS values account for only 0.01% of respondents.

Three further discontinuities are internal to KCHS. The current-drinking items were recoded in 2020, and the weighted prevalence rises from 72.5-75.4% before that year to 81.8-86.8% after it. The 2018 physical-activity module lacks the moderate-activity day count. Sleep duration is a weekday-only figure in 2017-2019 but a weekday-weighted seven-day average from 2020, whereas NHANES asks about weekdays. These three, together with the age top-code, the 2017 income refusal codes and the income quintile, were corrected in the analytic data before the primary analysis rather than carried as limitations; Table S10 quantifies singly each of the six tabulated corrections.

The preprocessing pipeline was fitted in the development training set and applied unchanged to the internal hold-out and to each external set. For the linear comparator, continuous predictors were median-imputed, categorical predictors mode-imputed, and binary predictors mode-imputed with an added missing indicator. The three ordinal scores (household income quintile, self-rated health and self-rated oral health) were median-imputed and standardized. In the post-pandemic cohort the income-to-poverty ratio is top-coded at 5.00 for 23.8% of respondents, hence the income quintile would collapse to four levels if the raw ratio were binned directly; the primary analysis instead recomputes a rank-based five-level score within each cohort, which restores five levels. The two alternative strategies examined in sensitivity analysis were missing indicators added for the continuous predictors, and single chained-equations imputation of the continuous predictors; weighted AUROC for both is given in Table S5. A check for silently omitted predictor columns was added to the pipeline after the data-integrity audit.

The amendment is summarized in English, with contextual notes marked as such, and the unmodified Korean original is released with the code, together with the crosswalk.

sections.verdict:
REVISE BEFORE USE. The condensation is largely sound and the arithmetic is clean, but two problems are must-fix and two more should be fixed before this goes to a journal.

WHAT PASSES.
Table 1 is byte-for-byte identical to the original, verified by diff over all 23 lines (caption, header, separator, 17 predictor rows, outcome row, race/ethnicity row). Not one variable name, code, threshold or definition moved.
Every prose number survives with its exact digits: 616 concepts, 175-variable extract, 265, 17 / seventeen, fourteen, odds ratio ~1.4, ~1.9-2.1, 18-item module, 80 years, 3.8%, up to 110, 2-14 hours, 0-23 hours, 0.01%, 2020, 72.5-75.4%, 81.8-86.8%, 2018, 2017-2019, 5.00, 23.8%. No rounding, no drift.
References [21] through [31] are all still cited, and this subsection remains their only citation site, so no reference is orphaned.
Hard rule 5 holds: the manuscript still says the protocol specified fourteen and that employment, self-rated oral health and food insecurity arrived by a dated amendment written before any model using them was fitted.
Hard rule 3 holds on the load-bearing sentence: "exhaustive with respect to the extract available at the time of the amendment rather than with respect to the full crosswalk" survives verbatim.
Named-section cross-references (Sensitivity Analyses), Table 1, Multimedia Appendix 1, Part A, Table S9, Table S10, Table S5 all resolve. Multimedia Appendix 1 does contain both Part A (appendix2_crosswalk.md) and Part B (appendix3_utility.md) per the manuscript's own Multimedia Appendix 1 description, so pointing relocated preprocessing detail at "Multimedia Appendix 1" is correct, not a broken reference.
Style scan of the manuscript-side text is clean: no we/our/ours/they/their/them/themselves, no "because", no result clause opening with "so" ("so that" purpose clauses are the original's own construction), no em dash, en dash or Unicode minus, no bold run-in labels. BMI is still expanded on first use, and the deletion of the prose predictor list did not orphan that expansion because the replacement carries "body mass index (BMI) [24]" ahead of Table 1.
Appendix-side claims check out against the sources: Table S5 does carry both the missing-indicator and the single chained-equations rows; Part A section A.5 does list each circular exclusion with its reason; "happiness index" matches Part A's own label for qoc_07z1, so it is not an invented specificity; Table S10 does tabulate exactly six corrections with three untabulated.

WHAT MUST BE FIXED.
Problems 1 and 2. The BMI deletion breaks a live pointer from Sensitivity Analyses, and "with contextual notes marked as such" is a transparency qualification about the amendment document that the writer wrongly declared as already standing word for word elsewhere. It stands nowhere in the manuscript now and nowhere in the appendix addition. Both fixes cost under fifteen words.

WHAT SHOULD BE FIXED.
Problems 3 and 4. The ordinal-score handling has been split into two model-specific claims the original did not make, which is the kind of thing a TRIPOD+AI reviewer reads closely; and the third retention criterion has been broadened past what the locked amendment says in Multimedia Appendix 1 section B.2.

MINOR.
Problems 5, 6 and 7 are a dropped qualifier, an over-reaching weighting preamble, and a heading that lands in the wrong Part.

ONE JUDGMENT CALL I AM NOT SCORING AS A DEFECT.
The linear comparator's imputation scheme moves entirely to the appendix. Hard rule 6 requires missing-data handling to stay in the Methods, and the primary model's handling does stay, in full. Moving the secondary model's scheme is defensible, but flag it to the writer so the choice is deliberate rather than incidental.

The writer's word-count defense is honest and correct: Table 1 plus footnotes account for 378 of the 967 words and are immovable under hard rules 1 and 4, and the prose reduction from 1222 to 589 words is the real measure. Nothing in the length argument excuses the two must-fix items, both of which are cheap to repair.

sections.heading: ### Model Development and Evaluation
sections.replacement:
No a priori sample-size calculation was performed; the samples are those the data allow, with the internal split described under Study Design and Data Sources and each external cohort being every eligible respondent in that cycle. What that supplies is reported instead: approximately 18,000 events in the training set, about 1,000 per candidate predictor and far above conventional events-per-predictor requirements, and approximately 3,600 in the hold-out. The external cohorts (728 events pre, 661 post) are the binding constraint on precision; discrimination therefore carries confidence intervals, and subgroup estimates are read as exploratory.

Three algorithms were considered, penalized logistic regression (elastic net), random forest and gradient boosting (LightGBM), in two selection steps confined to the KCHS training set. First, a randomized search over 24 LightGBM configurations crossed with two feature representations (main effects with and without four candidate interaction terms) fixed the gradient-boosting hyperparameters; the main-effects representation won, and the interactions did not improve cross-validated discrimination. Second, all three were tuned over comparable grids under one identical cross-validation protocol and compared at each algorithm's best configuration, following evidence that machine learning shows no systematic advantage over regression once validation bias is controlled [32]; only gradient boosting had received the preceding search, hence the comparison is like-for-like at tuned best rather than equal in cumulative effort. Both searches used individual-level cross-validation; the selection step may therefore be mildly optimistic, whereas the reported performance, which rests on the cluster-level separation of the hold-out and the parsimony selection set, is not.

The analysis plan fixed the primary-model rule in advance: highest cross-validated AUROC, with differences smaller than 0.005 treated as ties and broken by proximity of the calibration slope to 1, and only then by parsimony. The pipeline as executed ranked the algorithms on AUROC and then calibration slope without constructing the tie band; the plan's rule, checked retrospectively, reproduces the selected model (Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S9). Two departures are recorded in the same table: no class weighting, resampling or other imbalance correction was applied, the learner being fitted on the natural 3.6% event rate; and the searches were run single-pass rather than as 5-fold cross-validation repeated five times, which matters here, since the two leading algorithms differ by less than the tie band.

No NHANES data were used in fitting, tuning or selecting the primary model. The in-domain oracle reported under Testing Whether External Discrimination Can Be Raised Above ~0.77 is fitted on NHANES labels by design, as a diagnostic upper bound rather than a candidate model. The predictor set is the one exception: three of the seventeen items entered through a dated amendment written after the external result for the earlier set was known (Predictors and Harmonization). Complex-survey weights were handled by unweighted training with weighted evaluation (probed in sensitivity analysis). LightGBM was refitted on the full training set.

Performance was summarized by discrimination (AUROC and area under the precision-recall curve [AUPRC]), calibration, and operating characteristics, all complex-survey weighted. Calibration was assessed at the moderate level of the calibration hierarchy [33] and summarized by the calibration slope, calibration-in-the-large (CITL), the Brier score and expected calibration error (ECE), CITL being the intercept of a weighted offset logistic model. Ninety-five percent CIs are reported for AUROC, AUPRC and, externally, the calibration slope and CITL as transported and after recalibration; ECE, operating characteristics and net benefit are point estimates (ECE for the reason given with Table S16). CIs were obtained by a rescaled stratified cluster bootstrap with 1000 replicates [34], for cohort-level and subgroup estimates alike; bootstrap P values are two-sided, the smallest attainable value at 1000 replicates being reported as P<.001. Full development and resampling detail is given in Multimedia Appendix 1 and in the released analysis code and model card (see Data Availability).

A single operating threshold was fixed once in the development data at the predicted probability giving 85% sensitivity (0.02051) and applied unchanged to the internal hold-out and to both external cohorts; the external operating characteristics are therefore transported values rather than values selected in the cohort where reported. Clinical utility was assessed by weighted decision-curve analysis [35] over threshold probabilities of 0.02 to 0.30, each dataset carrying its own screen-all and screen-none default strategies.

## Supplementary methods for Model Development and Evaluation

This section carries the reproduction-level detail of the development, tuning and interval-construction procedures summarized in the Methods subsection Model Development and Evaluation. The external event counts also govern the precision of the external calibration estimates and of the decision-curve analysis.

The feature-representation and hyperparameter search compared 24 LightGBM configurations under single-pass 4-fold survey-weighted cross-validation in a 300,000-record subsample of the training set, crossed with two representations: main effects only, and main effects plus four candidate interaction terms (age×self-rated health, self-rated health×oral health, age×employment, income×employment). Those four terms were specified when the search was written and are not named in any earlier document (Table S9). The algorithm comparison then tuned elastic net, random forest and LightGBM over comparable 5-configuration grids under one protocol, single-pass 5-fold stratified cross-validation in a 200,000-record subsample of the training set scored by unweighted cross-validated AUROC, and compared each algorithm at its best configuration. Inside the plan's tie band the decision passes to the calibration slope, and the parsimony level of the rule is therefore never reached; the cross-validated values, the tie-band membership of each algorithm and the retrospective reconstruction of the rule are given in Table S9.

The primary model was refitted on the full 500,000-record training set with num_leaves 31, min_child_samples 1000, learning_rate 0.01, n_estimators 900, reg_alpha 1.0, reg_lambda 20, colsample_bytree 0.6, and subsample 0.6 with subsample_freq at its default of 0. The selected row-subsampling fraction is inactive in that configuration, given that the subsampling frequency was left at zero; the fitted model therefore uses all rows at every boosting iteration. The full search grids are specified in the released analysis code, and the selected configuration is recorded in the model card.

Calibration-in-the-large is estimated as the intercept of a weighted logistic model with the linear predictor entered as an offset, ie, with the slope fixed at 1; a positive value indicates that observed risk exceeds predicted risk. For the recalibrated columns of Table 2 the interval is obtained by refitting the intercept and slope inside every bootstrap replicate, so that the uncertainty of the update itself is carried; the wider fixed-update alternative is tabulated alongside it in Table S16. The interval for the difference in external AUROC between the two cycles is formed by differencing independently drawn replicate statistics rather than by pairing replicate indices, since the two cycles are disjoint samples. Bootstrap P values are read off the replicate distribution as twice the smaller tail proportion, and with 1000 replicates the smallest attainable value is reported as P<.001 rather than as an equality.

Bootstrap intervals are taken as the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the replicate distribution. Within each design stratum, *n*ₕ-1 primary sampling units are resampled with replacement and the survey weights rescaled by *n*ₕ/(*n*ₕ-1) times the selection count, following the replication approach cited in the manuscript. Rescaling is necessary given that most NHANES strata contain only two primary sampling units, for which an ordinary within-stratum cluster bootstrap understates variance. The implementation was verified against a closed-form design-based (linearized ultimate-cluster) standard error for weighted depression prevalence: bootstrap 0.00466 vs design 0.00471 in the pre-pandemic cycle and 0.00802 vs 0.00796 in the post-pandemic cycle, ie, agreement to within about 1.1%. For KCHS the stratum is defined as survey year crossed with the design stratum, owing to weight normalization within year and to the recurrence of stratum codes across years. Subgroup intervals are domain estimates: replicate weights are generated once on the full cohort design and then applied to each subgroup, rather than rebuilding the design after subsetting. Strata left with a single primary sampling unit are pooled into one pseudo-stratum, ensuring that the variance contribution of those strata is retained.

sections.heading: ### External Validation and Sensitivity Analyses
sections.replacement:
Geographic transportability was assessed by applying the KCHS-trained model to NHANES without refitting, and transportability across target periods by evaluating the same transported model separately in the pre- and post-pandemic cycles; since KCHS development pools 2017-2025 and spans both periods, the second comparison contrasts target periods rather than validating a model frozen before the later cycle. Recovery of calibration was quantified by out-of-sample intercept and slope updating, which corrects calibration without re-estimating any predictor effect [13,14] and is the conventional first step for a model moved to a new population [36]. Following the plan, three updates were applied, each cross-fitted over five folds grouped by primary sampling unit: intercept only, intercept plus slope, and one-parameter temperature scaling with the intercept fixed at zero. Table 2 tabulates the intercept-plus-slope result, the recommended update; the other two steps appear numerically in the Results.

Three further analyses were undertaken: interpretability, through global importance from tree-based Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) [37] and cross-survey rank concordance of predictor importance (Spearman correlation between KCHS and each NHANES cycle); fairness, through weighted subgroup AUROC and calibration slope across sex, age, education, and (NHANES) race/ethnicity, since algorithmic performance can differ systematically across groups [38]; and a parsimonious model for a low-burden self-administered form. For that model, predictor order and item count were both fixed inside the development training set, split into a 450,000-record fitting set and a 50,000-record selection set: predictors were entered in descending order of global SHAP importance, the model was refitted at every item count from 1 to 17, and the count was chosen on selection-set AUROC by the analysis plan's margin (the smallest set within 0.02 AUROC of the full model); a variant using a stricter 0.01 margin is flagged as post hoc (Multimedia Appendix 1, Part D). The internal hold-out and both NHANES cohorts served for evaluation only.

The model is intended as a triage aid for population-level screening programs and web or mobile self-assessment services, operated by public-health and primary-care services rather than by individuals acting alone, to prioritize who receives a full PHQ-9 and clinical follow-up. It is not a diagnostic instrument. Deployment presupposes local recalibration and, the household income predictor being a within-cohort rank, a local income distribution to rank against.

Sensitivity analyses were pre-specified, with further analyses added afterwards: the outcome cut-off (≥5 as well as ≥10), removal of the three added predictors (→14) and of food insecurity alone (→16), weighted versus unweighted training, two alternative imputation schemes, an age lower bound of 30 years applied to training *and* evaluation, a protocol-specified continuous-score analysis of how the model ranks the untransformed PHQ-9 total, and three alternative alcohol definitions. Weighted AUROC is tabulated in Multimedia Appendix 1, Table S5 for every specification apart from the continuous-score and alcohol analyses, reported in the Results text.

All analyses were performed in Python 3.14, with package versions listed in the model card. Net benefit is reported without intervals, since inference on a decision-analytic quantity answers a different question from the decision itself [39].

An adversarial data-integrity audit corrected three silent data-processing defects before final analysis: a fabricated living-alone constant in NHANES pre-pandemic, a post-pandemic physical-activity unit-field parsing error, and an income refusal code (77777) not treated as missing. Peer review identified four further defects, in the post-pandemic income quintile, the 2017 income refusal codes, the post-2020 drinking classification and the 2018 physical-activity indicator. The four peer-review defects were corrected in the primary analysis rather than carried forward as limitations; the defects and remedies are itemized in Multimedia Appendix 1, and Table S10 quantifies six corrections one at a time.

## Supplementary methods: external validation, recalibration, parsimony selection, and the data-integrity audit

This section carries the procedural detail underlying the manuscript subsection External Validation and Sensitivity Analyses. Nothing here alters any reported estimate.

Each of the three recalibration steps was cross-fitted over five folds grouped by primary sampling unit, so that no cluster contributes both to fitting an update and to evaluating it. The two-parameter intercept-plus-slope step is the Platt-type update.

Cross-survey rank concordance of predictor importance was undertaken as a mechanistic view of transportability. The fairness analysis was undertaken since algorithmic performance can differ systematically across groups even when overall accuracy is high.

For the parsimonious model, global Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) importance was computed on a random 20,000-record subsample of the 450,000-record fitting set. The search ran over every item count below 17 and did not impose the analysis plan's preferred 5-10 item range, which the selected count nonetheless satisfies. A variant using a stricter 0.01 margin is reported alongside the primary selection and is flagged as post hoc. Table S6 gives the full item-count trajectory.

The model is not a diagnostic instrument and does not replace clinical assessment. Since the household income predictor is a within-cohort rank, the 17-predictor model cannot be scored from one respondent's answers alone. The six-item form carries no such variable and no measured value; every one of its items is self-reportable in a web or mobile form, which is what makes it, rather than the full model, the version suited to remote and mobile delivery.

The self-report (KCHS) versus measured (NHANES) difference in body mass index is inherent to the data sources and is addressed in the harmonization cautions under Predictors and Harmonization and under Strengths and Limitations rather than by swapping measurements.

Complex-survey weighting, the rescaled stratified cluster bootstrap, the calibration measures, and decision-curve net benefit were implemented directly rather than through a survey-analysis package, and the implementations are released with the analysis code.

The adversarial data-integrity audit corrected three silent data-processing defects before the final analysis: living alone fabricated to a constant in NHANES pre-pandemic; post-pandemic physical activity coded 0 for every respondent through a unit-field parsing error; and an income refusal code (77777) not treated as missing, which had placed non-respondents in the top income quintile.

Peer review identified four further defects, all corrected in the primary analysis rather than carried forward as limitations: the income quintile collapsed to four levels post-pandemic through top-coding of the income-to-poverty ratio; the 2017 income refusal codes entered the highest quintile; post-2020 annual non-drinkers were coded as current drinkers (17.9% weighted of 2020-2025); and the 2018 physical-activity indicator used a different construct from adjacent years.

The remedies were: post-2020 annual non-drinkers recoded as non-drinkers; the 2018 activity indicator set to missing rather than silently redefined; the 2017 refusal codes masked and the income quintile recomputed as a rank-based five-level score within each survey year, which repairs both the four-level collapse and the scale mismatch between the 2017 ordinal field and the later monetary fields; sleep duration expressed on the weekday basis NHANES uses in every KCHS year; the age top-code aligned at 80 years in all cohorts; and the internal split rebuilt at cluster level.

Table S10 quantifies six of these corrections one at a time: the three questionnaire-driven KCHS discontinuities (the 2020 drinking recode, the 2018 activity fallback and the sleep alignment), the age alignment, the 2017 KCHS income refusal codes, and the income-quintile rebuild, the last of which also removes the four-level collapse in the post-pandemic cohort. Three corrections are not tabulated separately: the living-alone and physical-activity audit corrections, since in the uncorrected data the affected variable is constant rather than mismeasured, and the KCHS 77777 income refusal code, which is a missing-value declaration rather than a change of definition.
